127.title: Eid al-Fitr
127.hook: new clothes, the Eid prayer, visiting, sweets, and eid mubarak
127.howItsDone: On Eid al-Fitr, Muslims eat a few dates, wear their best clothes, say takbir on the way to the Eid prayer in a mosque or open ground, listen to the sermon, then spend the day visiting family and friends, sharing food and gifts, and greeting each other with eid mubarak.

segments.voice: Yesterday: zakat al-fitr, the charity of the fast's end, paid before the prayer. Your line was everyone eats on eid.

It's early morning, and the house smells like cardamom and fried dough. Kids are up early, in clothes that still have the tags on. Someone eats a few dates standing in the kitchen. On the way out, the family says it together, over and over: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar. In a park, a stadium, a big hall, thousands of people in their brightest colors line up in rows on the grass. After a month of empty afternoons, today no one is allowed to fast.
screen: `CARDAMOM AND FRIED DOUGH.` → `CLOTHES WITH THE TAGS STILL ON.` → `TODAY, NO ONE FASTS.`

segments.voice: Eid means a festival. Arabic dictionaries tie it to a root for returning: the day that comes back every year. Eid al-Fitr, the feast of breaking the fast, is the first day of the month after Ramadan, and much of it traces back to the Prophet ﷺ. Anas said in Bukhari that the Prophet wouldn't go out on Eid morning until he'd eaten some dates, an odd number of them. The fast is broken first thing, on purpose: fasting on Eid is forbidden. People wash, put on their best clothes, and go out to the Eid prayer, saying takbir along the way. The prayer is two rak'ahs, with extra takbirs, then a sermon. The Prophet would go by one road and come back by another; scholars give several reasons, and one is that more people along the way could greet him. Then the visiting, the food, the gifts for children, and the greetings: eid mubarak, a blessed Eid, and an older one reported from the companions, may Allah accept from us and from you. A small story in Bukhari shows what the day is for. On an Eid, the Prophet was resting at home while two girls were singing. Abu Bakr came in and scolded them: this, in the Prophet's house? The Prophet said: leave them, Abu Bakr. Every people has its festival, and this is our festival. Some readers take this to mean the joy isn't a lapse after the serious month, but part of the worship. And if, the week after, the prayers that came easily in Ramadan feel heavy again, that dip is common; day one hundred fifteen gave it a name. The door doesn't close with the month.
screen: `EID — THE DAY THAT RETURNS.` · `DATES FIRST; NO ONE FASTS.` · `ONE ROAD THERE, ANOTHER BACK.` · `LEAVE THEM, ABU BAKR.` · then, large: `THIS IS OUR FESTIVAL.`

segments.voice: Think back over the month: the moon, the dawn meal, the date at sunset, the nights, the tongue, the gift. Then think of one person to greet: if they're Muslim and it's Eid, eid mubarak; if not, or if it isn't Eid, a few words saying you're glad they exist. Let it be a small feast.
Eid. The festival that returns; Eid al-Fitr, the feast of breaking the fast, with dates, the prayer, visiting and sweets. Today's word.
Your line: a blessed feast. Every people has its festival, and this is ours. See you tomorrow.

128.title: The day of Arafah
128.hook: the pilgrims stand on the plain, and others fast the day
128.howItsDone: On the ninth of Dhu al-Hijjah, pilgrims stand on the plain of Arafah from midday to sunset in prayer and supplication, while many Muslims who are not on Hajj fast that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Eid, the feast at the end of Ramadan. Your line was a blessed feast.

The month of the pilgrimage, the ninth day. A wide, bare plain outside Mecca, a low hill in the middle, the sun climbing. A crowd of pilgrims reaching past the edge of sight, most dressed alike in plain white. Nobody is shopping. Nobody is sightseeing. From noon until sunset, they mostly just stand there, and ask. And far away, in kitchens and offices, other Muslims skip breakfast that morning, because they're fasting the same day.
screen: `A BARE PLAIN OUTSIDE MECCA.` → `MILLIONS IN WHITE, STANDING.` → `AND FAR AWAY, A FAST.`

segments.voice: Arafah is the ninth day of Dhu al-Hijjah, the month of the pilgrimage, and also the name of the plain itself. The Hajj has many rites: circling the Kaaba, walking between two hills, throwing pebbles, the sacrifice. But the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ summed it up in two words, reported by Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud: the Hajj is Arafah. Miss the standing on that plain, and in the view of the scholars, you've missed the Hajj. The standing is called wuquf. There's no fixed script for it. People pray, recite, weep, ask for forgiveness, ask for their families, in Arabic and in every other language. Tirmidhi reports that the best supplication is the supplication of the day of Arafah. Sahih Muslim adds that there's no day on which Allah frees more people from the Fire. It's a day of history too. Jabir's long account in Sahih Muslim has the Prophet giving his sermon at Arafah, on his farewell pilgrimage. And Bukhari reports that one line of the Qur'an came down on a Friday at Arafah: This day have I perfected your religion for you. Now the other half of the picture. For those at home, the tradition offers the fast. Sahih Muslim reports that fasting the day of Arafah is hoped to wipe away the sins of the year before and the year after. The pilgrims usually don't fast; they need their strength to stand. Many others do. One day, two ways of keeping it: standing on the plain, or fasting at your desk.
screen: `THE NINTH DAY, AND THE PLAIN.` · `THE HAJJ IS ARAFAH.` · `A FAREWELL, AND A FINISHED VERSE.` · `AT HOME: THE FAST.` · then, large: `ONE DAY, TWO WAYS TO KEEP IT.`

segments.voice: Sit or stand, whichever feels more like the plain, and choose one thing to give your full attention to, and only one: a person, a piece of work, a question you keep avoiding. If you pray, ask for help with it, in any words you have; if not, simply stay with it and let everything else wait.
Arafah. The ninth day of the pilgrimage month, and the plain where the pilgrims stand from noon to sunset. Today's word.
Your line: the standing day. From noon to sunset, just standing, and asking. That's day one hundred twenty-eight.

129.title: Eid al-Adha
129.hook: the feast of sacrifice remembers Ibrahim, and the meat is shared in thirds
129.howItsDone: On the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah Muslims pray the Eid prayer, and families who can afford it sacrifice an animal, often dividing the meat among the household, relatives and friends, and the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arafah, the plain where the pilgrims stand from noon to sunset. Your line was the standing day.

A freezer after a family celebration: foil packets, labeled in marker, stacked up, some already promised to other people. In some Muslim homes, the day after Arafah ends like that. It starts with the Eid prayer, early, in new or best clothes. Hugs, and eid mubarak again. Then a very old question: who gets the meat? This is the second of the two Eids, and the end of a run on this path that began with a new moon.
screen: `FOIL PACKETS, ALREADY PROMISED.` → `THE SECOND EID.` → `WHO GETS THE MEAT?`

segments.voice: Eid al-Adha means the feast of the sacrifice. It falls on the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah, the day after Arafah, while the pilgrims are finishing the Hajj. It remembers a story in Surah as-Saffat. Ibrahim sees in a dream that he is sacrificing his son, and tells him. The son answers: do what you are commanded; you'll find me, if Allah wills, among the patient. They both submit. Then Allah calls out to Ibrahim that he has already fulfilled the vision, and verse one hundred seven says: Then We ransomed him with a tremendous victim. The Qur'an doesn't name the son here. Tradition usually names Isma'il; some early scholars said Ishaq. Either way, the story ends with a life spared. In South Asia and elsewhere, the sacrifice is called qurbani, from the Arabic qurban, from a root meaning to be near: an offering is a way of drawing near. In Arabic it's usually called udhiyah. Families who can afford it sacrifice a sheep, a goat, or a share in a cow or camel, or pay someone to do it for them, often in a poorer country. Scholars differ on how binding it is: the Hanafi school calls it required for those who can afford it; the other major schools call it a strongly recommended sunnah. The Qur'an, in Surah al-Hajj, says the flesh and the blood don't reach Allah; what reaches Him is your devotion. So the meat is for people. The same surah says to eat of it and feed the poor, and a common recommendation divides it in three: a third for the household, a third for relatives and friends, a third for the poor. A feast that isn't finished until someone who has nothing gets a plate.
screen: `THE TENTH DAY: THE FEAST.` · `IBRAHIM, HIS SON, AND A RANSOM.` · `QURBAN — TO DRAW NEAR.` · `THE FLESH DOESN'T REACH ALLAH.` · then, large: `A THIRD FOR THE POOR.`

segments.voice: Picture your next meal and divide it in your mind: one part for your household, one for someone you know, a friend, a neighbor, a relative you haven't called, and one for someone you don't know who needs it. Watch each plate go to its place.
Qurbani. The sacrifice of Eid al-Adha, from a root meaning to be near, its meat shared with family, friends and the poor. Today's word.
Your line: a third for the poor. The flesh doesn't reach Allah; the devotion does. Day one hundred twenty-nine, done.

130.title: Just ask
130.hook: du'a is asking Allah directly, any time, in any language
130.howItsDone: Muslims make du'a at any time and in any language, often after the salat or with hands raised, asking Allah directly for their own needs and for others.

segments.voice: Yesterday: qurbani, the sacrifice of Eid al-Adha, shared three ways. Your line was a third for the poor.

One kind of prayer in Islam has no required form at all. No set words. No set language. No set time. You don't even need to face anywhere. You just talk. For weeks, this path has been teaching forms: the exact Arabic words, where the hands go, how many times to say glory, how many units at dawn. All that precision has a counterweight, and this is it.
screen: `ONE PRAYER WITH NO FORM AT ALL.` → `YOU JUST TALK.` → `AFTER WEEKS OF EXACT FORMS.`

segments.voice: The word is du'a, from an Arabic root that means to call, the way you'd call someone's name across a room. The salat, the five daily prayers, is the fixed form: set times, set movements, set words in Arabic. Du'a is the open one: asking Allah for something, directly, whenever you want. In Arabic, in English, in Urdu, in the half-sentences you'd use at three in the morning. In the usual view, it doesn't need wudu, a prayer mat, or a particular direction, though people often face the qiblah and raise their hands. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gave it a surprising rank. Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi report him saying: du'a is worship itself. Then he recited a verse, Surah Ghafir, forty, sixty: And your Lord hath said: Pray unto Me and I will hear your prayer. Not a formal request through the proper office. Pray unto Me. And the times it seems nothing happens? The hadith collections are honest about that. Bukhari reports that a person's du'a is answered as long as they don't grow impatient and say, I prayed and prayed and nothing came. A hadith in the Musnad of Ahmad says that a du'a asking for nothing sinful, and not for cutting family ties, is answered in one of three ways: given now, saved for the next life, or a harm of the same size quietly turned away. In that teaching, no such du'a is wasted. It may come back in a shape nobody ordered. Which leaves only the hard part: actually asking.
screen: `DU'A — TO CALL.` · `SALAT IS FIXED; DU'A IS OPEN.` · `DU'A IS WORSHIP ITSELF.` · `ANSWERED IN ONE OF THREE WAYS.` · then, large: `JUST ASK.`

segments.voice: Find the thing you actually want, not the polite version, small or large: sleep, a good conversation tomorrow, the test results. Put it into one plain sentence; if you pray, say it to Allah, in any language, out loud or silently, and if you don't, say it to yourself and notice how it feels to admit you want it. Then sit with it, and don't add anything.
Du'a. Calling on Allah directly, any time, in any language, asking for what you need. Today's word.
Your line: no du'a is wasted. Any language, any hour, any words. See you tomorrow.

131.title: When the heart is heavy
131.hook: a prophet who grieved out loud, a du'a against worry and grief, and help that isn't a lack of faith
131.howItsDone: Many Muslims say the Prophet's du'a against worry and grief in hard times, and many imams and Muslim counselors encourage therapy or medical care alongside prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: du'a, just asking, in any language, any time. Your line was no du'a is wasted.

An old man has wept so long over a lost son that his eyes have gone white. His other sons warn him he'll ruin his health, or die of it. He's a prophet: Ya'qub, Jacob, whose story you met in camp two. And he doesn't stop grieving, or pretend he's fine. He answers, in Pickthall's words: “I expose my distress and anguish only unto Allah.” A prophet, carrying something heavy, and saying so. Today: hamm.
screen: `EYES WHITE WITH GRIEF.` → `HE DOESN'T PRETEND.` → `MY DISTRESS, ONLY UNTO ALLAH.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an and the hadith don't treat sadness as a failure of faith. When the Prophet's ﷺ baby son Ibrahim was dying, the Prophet's eyes filled with tears. A companion was surprised. The Prophet said, in Bukhari: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord. Grief and faith, in the same breath. He also taught a du'a for exactly this weight. Anas, who served him for years, said in Bukhari that he often heard him say: Allahumma inni a'udhu bika minal-hammi wal-hazan. O Allah, I seek refuge in You from worry and from grief. Hamm is the weight of what might happen. Hazan is the ache of what already did. The du'a goes on through helplessness, laziness and the burden of debt: a list of very ordinary heaviness, said often. And he didn't make prayer the only medicine. Abu Dawud reports him telling people: seek treatment, servants of Allah, for Allah has not made a disease without making a remedy for it. Many Muslim scholars and counselors today apply that to the mind as well as the body: therapy and medicine alongside the du'a, not instead of it. Seeing a counselor is using the means Allah provides. So, said plainly: if the heaviness is more than a hard week, if it's taking your sleep or your hope, or if you've thought about not being here, please reach for help today. In the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help. Tell someone you trust. Ya'qub took his grief to Allah, and he still said it out loud.
screen: `TEARS AND FAITH, TOGETHER.` · `FROM WORRY, AND FROM GRIEF.` · `SEEK TREATMENT: THERE IS A REMEDY.` · `IF IT'S HEAVY: 988, OR LOCAL HELP.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, let your shoulders drop, and name, silently, the heaviest thing you're carrying today, just its name. As you breathe out, picture setting it down in front of you: not gone, just put down for a minute. If you pray, you can say the du'a, in Arabic or English: O Allah, I seek refuge in You from worry and from grief; if you don't, let each breath out be a little longer than the breath in.
Hamm. Worry, the weight of what might happen; in the Prophet's du'a it sits beside hazan, grief. Today's word.
Your line: the du'a and the doctor. Both are ways of asking for help, and you're allowed both. Go gently.

132.title: "I am near"
132.hook: when my servants ask about Me, I am near, I answer (2:186)
132.tomorrow: Good in this world and the next
132.howItsDone: Muslims often make du'a quietly, with the lips moving and little sound, following 2:186 and the Prophet's teaching that Allah is near and hears.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hamm, worry, and the Prophet's du'a against worry and grief. Your line was the du'a and the doctor.

On a bad phone line, people raise their voices. Across a parking lot, they shout and wave. To someone right beside them, in the dark at the end of a long day, they whisper. The volume of a voice carries a guess about distance: how far away the listener is. So here's a question for anyone who has ever prayed, or wanted to: how far away is the One you're talking to?
screen: `FAR AWAY, PEOPLE SHOUT.` → `RIGHT BESIDE THEM, THEY WHISPER.` → `HOW FAR AWAY IS HE?`

segments.voice: The answer is in Surah al-Baqarah, verse one hundred eighty-six, tucked in the middle of the verses about the Ramadan fast. And when My servants question thee concerning Me, then surely I am nigh. I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he crieth unto Me. Commentators point to how that verse is built. Elsewhere in the Qur'an, when people ask the Prophet a question, the answer begins with one word: Say. They ask you about the new moons; say. They ask you about wine; say. But here, when they ask about Allah Himself, there's no say. No go-between. The answer comes straight back: I am near. The Prophet ﷺ taught the same thing on a road. Bukhari and Muslim report that on a journey, the companions were calling out Allahu akbar at the tops of their voices. He told them: go easy on yourselves. You're not calling on someone deaf or absent. You're calling on One who hears, who is near, and who is with you. A verse in Surah Qaf puts it even closer: We are nearer to him than his jugular vein. The vein in your own neck. So in Islam you'll often see du'a made quietly, lips moving, almost no sound. Not because anything is secret, but because you don't shout at someone who's that close. Nearness here isn't a feeling you have to work up. It's a claim the text makes, whether you feel it or not.
screen: `2:186 — THEN SURELY I AM NIGH.` · `NO 'SAY': THE ANSWER COMES STRAIGHT.` · `NOT DEAF, NOT ABSENT.` · `NEARER THAN THE JUGULAR VEIN.` · then, large: `YOU DON'T SHOUT AT SOMEONE THAT CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Find the pulse in your neck, if you can, or at your wrist, and bring to mind the thing you asked for two days ago, or anything you'd like to ask. If you pray, say it, but barely: lips moving, almost no sound, as if to someone sitting right beside you; if you don't, whisper it to yourself just as quietly. Then stay in the quiet after it.
Jugular vein. The nearness verse in Surah Qaf says God is nearer to a person than this, the vein in their own neck.
Your line: he is near. Nearer than the vein in your own neck. That's day one hundred thirty-two.

133.title: Good in this world and the next
133.hook: the short du'a from the Qur'an: our Lord, give us good here and good hereafter (2:201)
133.howItsDone: Muslims often recite 2:201, rabbana atina fid-dunya hasanatan, at the end of their du'a, in the prayer, and while circling the Kaaba between the Yemeni corner and the Black Stone.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jugular vein, nearer than our own, the answer that comes with no go-between. Your line was he is near.

A man has grown so sick and thin that, in the report's words, he looks like a baby bird. The Prophet ﷺ visits him and asks what he's been praying for. His answer is startling. Some people, when they finally get the chance to ask for something, ask for too little: just get me through this week. Others turn it into a grand, dramatic bargain. Both are very human. This man, in a story from Sahih Muslim, did the dramatic kind. And the Prophet gave him a better prayer.
screen: `A MAN LIKE A BABY BIRD.` → `TOO LITTLE, OR TOO DRAMATIC.` → `THE PROPHET GIVES HIM A BETTER ONE.`

segments.voice: The man said: I've been asking Allah, whatever punishment You'd give me in the next life, give it to me now, in this one. He was trying to get it over with. The Prophet told him he couldn't bear that, and asked why he didn't say instead the du'a from Surah al-Baqarah, verse two hundred one. In Pickthall's translation: Our Lord! Give unto us in the world that which is good and in the Hereafter that which is good, and guard us from the doom of Fire. The report says the man prayed it, and Allah healed him. In Arabic it begins rabbana atina fid-dunya hasanatan: our Lord, give us in this world good. The word for good, hasanah, shares its root letters with ihsan, excellence, and husn, beauty. It isn't narrow. Commentators such as Ibn Kathir read good in this world widely: health, knowledge, a good spouse, honest provision. The verse doesn't choose; it leaves the space open. Notice its shape. In the verse just before, the Qur'an describes people who only ask, give us in this world, and stop. This du'a asks for both. Not this life instead of the next, or the next instead of this one. Good here, and good there. Anas, who served the Prophet, said in Bukhari that this was the du'a he made most often. Abu Dawud reports the Prophet saying it while circling the Kaaba, between two of its corners, and pilgrims say it there still. Some people close their own du'a with it, as a way of asking for everything they forgot to mention.
screen: `PUNISH ME NOW, HE PRAYED.` · `SAY 2:201 INSTEAD.` · `HASANAH — A WIDE WORD FOR GOOD.` · `BOTH, NOT ONE OR THE OTHER.` · then, large: `GOOD HERE, AND GOOD THERE.`

segments.voice: If you like, raise your hands, palms up. If you pray, say the verse once, slowly: rabbana atina fid-dunya hasanatan, wa fil-akhirati hasanatan, wa qina 'adhaban-nar; or in English: our Lord, give us good in this world, and good in the hereafter, and guard us from the Fire. If you don't pray, think of one good you want here and one good you'd want to last beyond it, and hold both at once.
Hasanah, good: the word at the heart of the short du'a in Surah al-Baqarah, asking for good here, good hereafter, and protection.
Your line: good here, good there. Not one or the other: both. Day one hundred thirty-three, done.
